full_judgment:
21. It is true that there has been a great delay in propounding the will. It was executed in 1921 and was presented first for granting probate in Civil Suit No. 8 of 1945 but was withdrawn in 1946 with liberty to file a fresh petition for probate. After the death of the executor plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed the present application for Letters of Administration on 5.9.69. The delay has been claimed to raise suspicion as to the genuineness of the will. As regards the evidence relating to the execution and attestation of the will the appellant's Counsel tried his best to show that it was not sufficient to prove them, particularly with reference to the requirements laid down in section 63 (c) of the Succession Act as to proof of execution and attestation of a will. The appellant's Counsel repeatedly asserted that the mode of execution of a will prescribed by the aforesaid provisions was not complied with in executing the will in question. As already mentioned, we were taken through the evidence: both oral and documentary and considering them as well as the time gap between the execution of the will and the evidence recorded in the suit, particularly the evidence of P.Ws. 3 and 4 and the contents of the will itself, we find it difficult to discard them, So far as the execution and attestation are concerned, mode of execution of a will as laid down in section 63 (c) is distinguishable from the evidence as to the strict compliance with the technicalities prescribed thereunder. Broadly viewing the evidence of P Ws. 3 and 4 and the will in question, it appears that its execution and attestation have been proved. If Pitambar and the scribe who wrote the will as well as signed Pitambar's name thereon were seen to be present in Pitambar's house at the time the will was created, which are testified by P.W.4, Sarada Charan Chakraborty, evidence regarding the meticulous observance of the sequence in which a will is to be executed is bound to be somewhat blurred after the lapse of nearly half a century. The naturalness of the whole transaction visibly appears from the evidence of P.Ws. 3 and 4. 

 22. I now propose to refer to a few decisions on the requirements of law relating to proof of a will, They are concerning the execution and attestation of a will and also some' other facto.rs which are relevant for establishing the genuineness of such a document. 

 23. These decisions refer to various requirements of law as to the mode of proving a will, such as the effect of delay in applying for probate, the onus of proof, the need for considering every circumstance of legitimate suspicion and compliance with the provisions of law as to the execution and attestation of the will, The primary requirement in the matter of proving a will is that the party who sets up a will must be able to show that the testator was of sound disposing mind at the time of execution of will. Thus, in Munnalal vs. Mst. Kashibai, AIR 1947 PC 15, Sir John Beaumont observed: 

 "A party setting up a will is required to prove that the testator was of sound disposing mind when he made his will but, in the absence of any evidence as to the state of the testator's mind, proof that he has executed a will rational in character in the presence of witnesses must lead to a presumption that he was of sound mind, and understood, what he was about." 

 24. Burden of proof lies on the party propounding a will who must, therefore, satisfy the court that the will reflects the last wishes of the testator. If it is found that he is taking a benefit under, the will the court should be cautious and carefully examine the evidence in support of the will because he is likely to have a strong motive in proving the execution of the will. His evidence must be received with a bit of caution than that of a disinterested witness. A court is expected to be less ready to accept his evidence unless corroborated. In support of these propositions reliance was placed on the case of Harmes vs. Hinkson, (1945) 50 CWN 895.
